ANCILLARY PROBATE FOR OUT-OF-STATE PROPERTY — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · sister-state personal representative

PROPOSED PETITIONER — INFORMATION AND DECLARATION IN SUPPORT OF ANCILLARY PETITION
I, Jordan Lee, am sister-state personal representative of Taylor Morgan, who died on January 1, 2026 while domiciled in Nevada. Taylor Morgan's estate is the subject of a primary probate or estate administration proceeding outside California: Clark County District Court, Case No. P-26-000000. Taylor Morgan also owned real property located in California, described as: 123 Main St, San Diego, CA 92101. This declaration provides background information for use with an actual petition for ancillary administration, to be filed in the California superior court for San Diego County under Probate Code Part 13 (commencing with Section 12500), for probate of Taylor Morgan's will and/or appointment of a California personal representative with respect to the California property described above. The character and estimated value of that California property is: 50,000. This declaration is not itself a court filing, and signing it does not open an ancillary administration proceeding, admit any will to probate in California, appoint Jordan Lee — or anyone else — as a California personal representative, or transfer or distribute any interest in the California property described above. Only a California court order issued after the statutory ancillary petition, notice, and hearing process described in this document can do that, and only the subsequent issuance of California letters gives a California personal representative actual authority to act with respect to the California property.

WHY A SEPARATE CALIFORNIA PROCEEDING IS NEEDED — PROPERTY LOCATION, NOT A FREE-STANDING 'SITUS' STATUTE
Real property is generally administered, for probate purposes, under the law of the state where it is physically located, regardless of the decedent's domicile — a principle usually described as the property's "situs." California's Probate Code does not contain a single section that states this situs principle as a free-standing rule; instead, California implements it through its jurisdiction and venue provisions. Probate Code § 7051 provides that if Taylor Morgan was domiciled in California at the time of death, the proper county for estate-administration proceedings is the county of Taylor Morgan's domicile, regardless of where Taylor Morgan died. Probate Code § 7052 supplies the converse rule for a nondomiciliary decedent: if Taylor Morgan was not domiciled in California at the time of death, the proper county for proceedings under the Probate Code is instead tied to where Taylor Morgan died (if property is located in that county) or, otherwise, to any county in which Taylor Morgan's property is located — venue that turns on property location rather than domicile. Probate Code § 12505 in turn defines a "nondomiciliary decedent," for purposes of the ancillary administration provisions discussed elsewhere in this document, as "a person who dies domiciled in a sister state or foreign nation."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "If the decedent was domiciled in this state at the time of death, the proper county for proceedings concerning administration of the decedent’s estate is the county in which the decedent was domiciled, regardless of where the decedent died."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 7051 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 7051 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=7051.)
  "If the decedent was not domiciled in this state at the time of death, the proper county for proceedings under this code concerning the administration of the decedent’s estate is one of the following: (a) If property of the nondomiciliary decedent is located in the county in which the nondomiciliary decedent died, the county in which the nondomiciliary decedent died. (b) If no property of the nondomiciliary decedent is located in the county in which the nondomiciliary decedent died or if the nondomiciliary decedent did not die in this state, any county in which property of the nondomiciliary decedent is located, regardless of where the nondomiciliary decedent died."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 7052 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 7052 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=7052.)
  "“Nondomiciliary decedent” means a person who dies domiciled in a sister state or foreign nation."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 12505 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 12505 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=12505.)
  Known gap: This corrects an assumption in the original research brief: California's Probate Code does not state the situs principle as an explicit, free-standing declarative rule (e.g., a section reading "real property is governed by the law of the state where located"); the principle is instead implemented structurally, through the jurisdiction and venue provisions cited here (§§ 7051-7052) and the ancillary-administration framework described in this document's other clauses. This document does not independently verify a California case establishing the situs principle as a matter of common law or conflict-of-laws doctrine; it relies solely on how these statutory venue provisions are written. This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of California's own venue rules for estate administration — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's property, and not a claim that California's ancillary administration provisions apply to a California domiciliary's property located in a different state (that question is governed by the other state's law, not California's Probate Code, and is outside the scope of this document, which addresses only California as the ancillary jurisdiction). This clause cites three different statutory sections (§ 7051, § 7052, and § 12505); no single section is cited more than once in this clause.

CALIFORNIA'S ANCILLARY ADMINISTRATION PROCEDURE — WHO MAY PETITION, AND WHAT MUST (AND NEED NOT) BE SHOWN
Probate Code § 12501 defines "ancillary administration" as "proceedings in this state for administration of the estate of a nondomiciliary decedent." Probate Code § 12510 provides that any interested person, or a sister state or foreign nation personal representative, may commence an ancillary administration proceeding in California by a petition to the court for either or both of: probate of Taylor Morgan's will, and appointment of a local (California) personal representative. Where Taylor Morgan's will has already been admitted to probate in the sister state or foreign nation of domicile, Probate Code § 12520(a) allows that will to be probated in the California ancillary proceeding under a separate, comity-based procedure described elsewhere in Part 13 of the Probate Code; where the will has not been admitted to probate elsewhere, or does not satisfy that procedure's requirements, § 12520(b) provides that the will may instead be probated in the ancillary proceeding under the same general procedure — Part 2 of Division 7, commencing with Section 8000 — that governs an ordinary California probate petition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Ancillary administration” means proceedings in this state for administration of the estate of a nondomiciliary decedent."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 12501 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 12501 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=12501.)
  "Any interested person, or a sister state or foreign nation personal representative, may commence an ancillary administration proceeding by a petition to the court for either or both of the following: (a) Probate of the nondomiciliary decedent’s will. (b) Appointment of a local personal representative."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 12510 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 12510 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=12510.)
  "(a) If a nondomiciliary decedent’s will has been admitted to probate in a sister state or foreign nation and satisfies the requirements of this article, probate of the will in an ancillary administration proceeding is governed by this article. (b) If a nondomiciliary decedent’s will has been admitted to probate in a sister state or foreign nation, but does not satisfy the requirements of this article, the will may be probated in an ancillary administration proceeding pursuant to Part 2 (commencing with Section 8000)."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 12520 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 12520 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=12520.)
  Known gap: This corrects an assumption in the original research brief: § 12510's own text does not require the petitioner to show, as a precondition to commencing a California ancillary administration proceeding, that a domiciliary or primary probate proceeding has already been opened (or completed) in the decedent's state or country of domicile. A domiciliary proceeding's existence and outcome matter for two narrower, related purposes addressed elsewhere in this document: whether the streamlined comity procedure of § 12520(a) is available for probating a will already admitted elsewhere, and who has statutory priority to be appointed as the California ancillary personal representative. The ancillary petition under § 12510 itself, however, may be commenced by any interested person, or by a sister state or foreign nation personal representative, without a threshold showing that a domiciliary proceeding exists. This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of California's own ancillary-administration procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate, and not a claim that any specific estate qualifies for or requires this procedure. This clause cites three different statutory sections (§ 12501, § 12510, and § 12520); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. This document is informational: it does not itself open an ancillary administration proceeding, admit any will to probate in California, or appoint any personal representative — only a California court order issued after the statutory petition, notice, and hearing process can do that.

THE CALIFORNIA ANCILLARY PERSONAL REPRESENTATIVE'S AUTHORITY, AND PRIORITY FOR APPOINTMENT
Probate Code § 12530 provides that, except to the extent Part 13 of the Probate Code otherwise provides, ancillary administration of Taylor Morgan's estate "is subject to all other provisions of this code concerning the administration of the decedent's estate, including, but not limited to, opening estate administration, inventory and appraisal, creditor claims, estate management, independent administration, compensation, accounts, payment of debts, distribution, and closing estate administration." Probate Code § 12512 similarly provides that notice of an ancillary administration proceeding is given, and the same proceedings are had, as in an ordinary California probate of a will or appointment of a personal representative for a person who died domiciled in California — except as Article 2 (the will-probate procedure discussed elsewhere in this document, commencing with § 12520) otherwise provides. On the question of who is appointed, § 12513 gives a specific priority: if Taylor Morgan died while domiciled in a sister state, a personal representative already appointed by a court of Taylor Morgan's domicile has priority over all other persons for appointment as the California ancillary personal representative — except where Taylor Morgan's will nominates a different person for that California role — and that domiciliary personal representative may instead nominate another person to serve, with that nominee taking the same priority.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Except to the extent otherwise provided in this chapter, ancillary administration of a decedent’s estate is subject to all other provisions of this code concerning the administration of the decedent’s estate, including, but not limited to, opening estate administration, inventory and appraisal, creditor claims, estate management, independent administration, compensation, accounts, payment of debts, distribution, and closing estate administration."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 12530 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 12530 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=12530.)
  "Notice of an ancillary administration proceeding shall be given and, except as provided in Article 2 (commencing with Section 12520), the same proceedings had as in the case of a petition for probate of a will or appointment of a personal representative of a person who dies domiciled in this state."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 12512 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 12512 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=12512.)
  "If the decedent dies while domiciled in a sister state, a personal representative appointed by a court of the decedent’s domicile has priority over all other persons except where the decedent’s will nominates a different person to be the personal representative in this state. The sister state personal representative may nominate another person as personal representative and the nominee has the same priority as the sister state personal representative."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 12513 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 12513 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=12513.)

This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of California's own ancillary-administration procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate. This clause cites three different statutory sections (§ 12530, § 12512, and § 12513); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. This document is informational: it does not itself appoint any personal representative or determine priority for any specific estate — only a California court order does that.

DISTRIBUTION OF CALIFORNIA ASSETS AFTER ANCILLARY ADMINISTRATION — TWO STATUTORY PATHS, NOT ONE
California's Probate Code provides for two distinct paths by which Taylor Morgan's California assets can be distributed following ancillary administration. By default, under Probate Code § 12530, distribution of Taylor Morgan's California property proceeds under the general Probate Code distribution provisions applicable to any California estate — that is, under Taylor Morgan's will or, if Taylor Morgan died intestate, under California's intestate succession rules — the same as in an ordinary, non-ancillary probate. Separately, Probate Code § 12540(a) gives the court discretion, in an ancillary administration proceeding, to instead order preliminary or final distribution of all or part of Taylor Morgan's personal property located in California to the sister state personal representative, "if distribution is in the best interest of the estate or interested persons." Where distribution to the sister state personal representative is necessary, § 12541 allows real property in Taylor Morgan's estate to be sold, with the court ordering the sale proceeds — rather than the real property itself — distributed to the sister state personal representative, using the same procedures that apply to other sales of a decedent's real property. Finally, § 12542 provides that if the estate in Taylor Morgan's sister state of domicile is insolvent, distribution of the property described in this article may be made only to the sister state personal representative, and not directly to beneficiaries.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Except to the extent otherwise provided in this chapter, ancillary administration of a decedent’s estate is subject to all other provisions of this code concerning the administration of the decedent’s estate, including, but not limited to, opening estate administration, inventory and appraisal, creditor claims, estate management, independent administration, compensation, accounts, payment of debts, distribution, and closing estate administration."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 12530 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 12530 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=12530.)
  "If a person dies while domiciled in a sister state, the court in an ancillary administration proceeding may make an order for preliminary or final distribution of all or part of the decedent’s personal property in this state to the sister state personal representative if distribution is in the best interest of the estate or interested persons."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 12540(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 12540(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=12540.)
  "If necessary to make distribution pursuant to this article, real property in the nondomiciliary decedent’s estate may be sold and the court may order the proceeds to be distributed to the sister state personal representative. The sale shall be made in the same manner as other sales of real property of a decedent."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 12541 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 12541 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=12541.)
  "If the nondomiciliary decedent’s estate in the sister state where the decedent was domiciled is insolvent, distribution may be made only to the sister state personal representative and not to the beneficiaries."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 12542 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 12542 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=12542.)
  Known gap: This corrects an assumption embedded in the original research brief's framing (direct distribution under the will or intestate succession, versus transmission to the domiciliary representative, as though only one applies): both paths exist under California law, and which one a court uses is discretionary rather than automatic. The default, absent a court order under Article 4, is direct California distribution under § 12530's general rule; transmission of personal property (or real property sale proceeds) to the sister state personal representative under §§ 12540-12542 requires an affirmative court finding that it serves the best interest of the estate or interested persons, and — for real property specifically — the statute's text authorizes selling the property and distributing the proceeds, not distributing the real property itself in kind, to the sister state personal representative. This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of California's own ancillary-administration distribution rules — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate, and not a claim that a court will order any particular distribution in any specific case. This clause cites four different statutory sections (§ 12530, § 12540, § 12541, and § 12542); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. This document is informational: it does not itself order any distribution — only a California court order does that.

A SIMPLIFIED ALTERNATIVE TO ANCILLARY PROBATE FOR A NONRESIDENT DECEDENT'S SMALLER CALIFORNIA PROPERTY
Ancillary probate is not required for every nonresident decedent's California property, regardless of value. For California real property specifically, Probate Code § 13200(a) allows a successor of Taylor Morgan to file a small-value real property affidavit — no sooner than six months after Taylor Morgan's death — in the superior court for the county in which the real property is located, when Taylor Morgan was not domiciled in California at the time of death. That subdivision requires the affidavit to state, among other things, that "[n]o proceeding is now being or has been conducted in California for administration of the decedent's estate," or, alternatively, that "the decedent's personal representative has consented in writing to use of the procedure provided by this chapter." Separately, for California personal property, Probate Code § 12570 allows a sister state personal representative to use the ordinary personal-property small-estate affidavit procedure of Probate Code § 13100 — without petitioning for ancillary administration at all — whenever Taylor Morgan's California property "satisfies the requirements of Section 13100," which itself applies (subject to its own dollar threshold and 40-day waiting period) when "the gross value of the decedent's real and personal property in this state does not exceed one hundred sixty-six thousand two hundred fifty dollars ($166,250), as adjusted periodically."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "No sooner than six months from the death of a decedent, a person or persons claiming as successor of the decedent to a particular item of property that is real property may file in the superior court in the county in which the decedent was domiciled at the time of death, or if the decedent was not domiciled in this state at the time of death, then in any county in which real property of the decedent is located, an affidavit in the form prescribed by the Judicial Council pursuant to Section 1001 stating all of the following"
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13200(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 13200(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13200.)
  "If a nondomiciliary decedent’s property in this state satisfies the requirements of Section 13100, a sister state personal representative may, without petitioning for ancillary administration, use the affidavit procedure provided by Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 13100) of Part 1 of Division 8 to collect personal property of the decedent."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 12570 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 12570 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=12570.)
  "Excluding the property described in Section 13050 and any property included in a petition filed under Section 13151, if the gross value of the decedent’s real and personal property in this state does not exceed one hundred sixty-six thousand two hundred fifty dollars ($166,250), as adjusted periodically in accordance with Section 890, and if 40 days have elapsed since the death of the decedent, the successor of the decedent may, without procuring letters of administration or awaiting probate of the will, do any of the following with respect to one or more particular items of property"
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13100 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 13100 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13100.)
  Known gap: This confirms, with an important nuance, the framing in the original research brief: California does offer a simplified, non-ancillary alternative for a nonresident decedent's California property, but the statute provides it through two different mechanisms depending on the type of property, not one unified small-estate procedure. The real-property affidavit of § 13200 is available for a nonresident decedent's California real property on its own terms — it expressly addresses a decedent "not domiciled in this state" — independent of the cross-reference in Probate Code Part 13's ancillary-administration chapter, which instead reaches only the personal-property affidavit of § 13100 through § 12570, and is limited there to use by a sister state personal representative rather than any successor. Both mechanisms remain unavailable, per their own text, once a California administration proceeding is pending or has been conducted, unless the decedent's personal representative has consented in writing — so if ancillary probate has already been opened for the decedent's California property, these simplified alternatives are foreclosed absent that consent. This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of California's own small-estate and ancillary-administration procedures — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate, and not a claim that any specific estate qualifies for these procedures, which also depend on statutory dollar thresholds and waiting periods this clause does not fully restate. This clause cites three different statutory sections (§ 13200(a), § 12570, and § 13100); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. This document is informational: it does not itself transfer any property or determine whether a specific estate qualifies for these procedures.

Executed on October 1, 2026 at San Diego, California.

By default, under Probate Code § 12530, distribution of Taylor Morgan's California property proceeds under the general Probate Code distribution provisions applicable to any California estate — that is, under Taylor Morgan's will or, if Taylor Morgan died intestate, under California's intestate succession rules — the same as in an ordinary, non-ancillary probate. Separately, Probate Code § 12540(a) gives the court discretion, in an ancillary administration proceeding, to instead order preliminary or final distribution of all or part of Taylor Morgan's personal property located in California to the sister state personal representative, "if distribution is in the best interest of the estate or interested persons." Where distribution to the sister state personal representative is necessary, § 12541 allows real property in Taylor Morgan's estate to be sold, with the court ordering the sale proceeds — rather than the real property itself — distributed to the sister state personal representative, using the same procedures that apply to other sales of a decedent's real property. Finally, § 12542 provides that if the estate in Taylor Morgan's sister state of domicile is insolvent, distribution of the property described in this article may be made only to the sister state personal representative, and not directly to beneficiaries.
